newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Unions say workers join Belgrade demonstrations.
newsitem.headline: Unions say workers join Belgrade demonstrations.

text.p: Independent trade union leaders claimed on Wednesday that thousands of workers had joined street protests against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic but admitted many were frightened to demonstrate.

Leaders of the association of independent trade unions said 10,000 workers were taking part in daily student and opposition demonstrations against the refusal of Milosevic's ruling socialists to accept opposition victories in local elections.
The West has supported demonstrations by up to 150,000 people a day in Belgrade but the mainly middle class protestors have failed to attract significant support from workers.
"They are afraid to march because they say their bosses will recognise them and they will be kicked out of their factories," a union official said.
Independent unions claimed some of their 40,000 members in Belgrade had begun strike action citing the alleged election fraud among their grievances as well as pay.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties on Tuesday lost its last legal appeal against the outcome of the November 17 elections when the Yugoslav federal supreme court refused to intervene.
Political sources said Zajedno urgently needed to find new ways of maintaining the momentum of its campaign to drive Milosevic from power.
The United States and other western governments have denounced Milosevic and threatened him with unspecified reprisals if he uses force against the demonstrators.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher accused the former communist Milosevic of running "an unreformed dictatorship" but did not spell out whether Washington would try to reimpose sanctions on Serbia or what other measures might be taken.
President Bill Clinton on Tuesday urged that "the voice of the people should be heard.
U.N. sanctions against Yugoslavia during the Bosnian war also targeted Montenegro, Serbia's partner in the Yugoslav federation, which is not involved in the election conflict.
With Montenegro excluded from any renewal of sanctions, making the measures stick would be even harder than before when all Serbia's neighbours turned a blind eye to smuggling on a huge scale.
The lack of concrete moves against Milosevic by the West has increased Zajedno's opposition suspicions that despite the bluster, Washington and its allies do not seriously want to destabilise him.

Although the socialists used the courts to uphold the replacement by socialists of disqualified Zajedno councillors, an allied party of the socialists hinted that a negotiated settlement was possible.
The Yugoslav United Left (JUL), which fought the elections in coalition with the Socialists, said a "common solution" was possible.
JUL president Ljubisa Ristic told the independent news agency Beta that "readiness for talks and agreements will mature slowly."
"In politics...there is a need to come to a solution so I believe that such a common solution will be reached however difficult, ugly, unpleasant and dramatic the situation may now seem."
